# 3.1 Sampling distribution {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The decomposition that is all of inference

Substitute $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ into $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$:

$$\hat\beta = \beta + (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \varepsilon$$

::: {.check}
Everything that follows depends only on what you are willing to assume about $\varepsilon$.
:::

## Unbiasedness

$$\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta \mid X] = \beta + (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = \beta$$

using only **strict exogeneity**.

::: {.muted}
Note what is *not* needed: no homoskedasticity, no normality, no independence.
:::

## Variance, under homoskedasticity

$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta \mid X) = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X) X (X^\top X)^{-1} = \sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}$$

## The form worth memorising

For a single coefficient:

$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n \cdot \mathrm{Var}(x_j) \cdot (1 - R_j^2)}$$

where $R_j^2$ is the $R^2$ from regressing $x_j$ on all other regressors.

## Four levers

::: {.tight}
- $\sigma^2$ — **noise**
- $n$ — **sample size**
- $\mathrm{Var}(x_j)$ — **variation in the regressor**
- $1/(1-R_j^2)$ — **redundancy**: the variance inflation factor
:::

::: {.check}
That last factor is the price of collinearity — and precisely what regularisation in Session 05
proposes to pay differently.
:::

# 3.2 Gauss–Markov {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The theorem

> Under assumptions 1–4, $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ has the **smallest variance in the class of linear
> unbiased estimators**.

## Proof sketch

Let $\tilde\beta = Cy$ be any linear unbiased estimator; write

$$C = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top + D$$

Unbiasedness forces $DX = 0$. Then

$$\mathrm{Var}(\tilde\beta) = \sigma^2\big[(X^\top X)^{-1} + DD^\top\big] \succeq \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta)$$

since $DD^\top \succeq 0$. $\blacksquare$

## The crucial caveat

BLUE is a guarantee **within the class of unbiased estimators**.

::: {.warn}
Sessions 04 and 05 show that deliberately accepting bias can lower total error. Gauss–Markov does
not forbid this. It simply does not apply.
:::

# 3.3 When assumption 4 fails {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The sandwich is always correct

$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta \mid X) = (X^\top X)^{-1} \Big( X^\top \Omega X \Big) (X^\top X)^{-1}$$

with $\Omega = \mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon \mid X)$.

::: {.check}
$\hat\beta$ never changes. Only your claimed precision does.
:::

## Heteroskedasticity-robust — White / HC1

Estimate $\Omega$ by

$$\mathrm{diag}(\hat\varepsilon_i^2)$$

with a small-sample correction $n/(n-p)$.

## Cluster-robust

If errors are correlated within groups $g$ — firms, regions, countries:

$$\hat\Omega = \sum_g \hat\varepsilon_g \hat\varepsilon_g^\top$$

::: {.warn}
Requires **many** clusters. With fewer than roughly **40**, inference is unreliable — and a
30-country panel sits below that line.
:::

## The practical rule

> **Cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned.**

::: {.muted}
Not at the level that gives the smallest standard error. State the level in your table note: two
papers can both write "robust standard errors" and mean different things.
:::

# 3.4 Omitted variable bias {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The formula

True model $y = X_1\beta_1 + X_2\beta_2 + u$, but you estimate on $X_1$ alone. Let $\delta$ be the
coefficient matrix from regressing $X_2$ on $X_1$. Then

$$\mathbb{E}[\hat\beta_1] = \beta_1 + \delta \beta_2$$

## Sign the bias with two questions

::: {.tight}
1. How does the omitted variable relate to **my regressor**? → $\delta$
2. How does it relate to the **outcome**? → $\beta_2$
:::

**Same sign in both → upward bias.**

::: {.check}
Answer both in writing *before* you estimate. The single most useful discipline in applied work,
and it is free.
:::

# 3.5 A Mincer coefficient {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What it identifies

$$\log w_i = \alpha + \rho\, S_i + \gamma_1 X_i + \gamma_2 X_i^2 + \varepsilon_i$$

$\rho$ is often read as "the return to a year of schooling".

## Strictly

> The mean log-wage difference associated with an additional year of schooling **among people who
> are otherwise identical on the included covariates**.

::: {.warn}
Unobserved ability, selection into schooling and measurement error all break the causal reading.
Session 10 gives tools that take this seriously.
:::

::: {.check}
Today the discipline is simply to **say precisely what you have estimated**.
:::

# The practice {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you do

::: {.tight}
1. Fit the specification on the practice data; inspect residuals against fitted values
2. Compute classical, HC1 and cluster-robust standard errors side by side
3. Name a confounder, **sign its bias**, then test your prediction
4. Report the coefficient with the cluster level named
:::

::: {.warn}
Report $n$ **and** the number of clusters. Both are true; only one governs precision.
:::

## The two-minute report

**One slide. Three sentences.**

::: {.tight}
1. **What I did** — the specification, and what you clustered on
2. **The number** — with its interval
3. **The catch** — the confounder you could not rule out, and its direction
:::

::: {.check}
Full brief: [`02-practice/README.md`](02-practice/README.md)
:::
